extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, research funders, and researchers involved in peer review and scholarly communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how scholarly peer review should be organised and practised, covering review models, transparency, reproducibility, post-publication commentary, training and incentives for reviewers. Aimed at informing publishers, editors and policy-makers about options and trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and cost-effectiveness of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the expenditure of time and effort on editorial and peer review work is efficient and cost-effective given high monetary and opportunity costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that peer review costs are borne largely by researchers and institutions; publishers should pay attention to reducing unnecessary burden while retaining review quality. High costs warrant exploring changes to models and procedures to improve efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimising publication delays and redundant reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce delays caused by reviewers completing reviews and authors responding, and by sequential submissions that trigger multiple rounds of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include transferring reviews between journals (within or across publishers), developing cascading/portable-review systems, or considering more rapid publication with post-publication review. Authors should be offered choice over transfers; editors value independence and may request additional reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing unfairness and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Tackle scope for bias on grounds such as sex, race, nationality, or field of study, which can arise particularly in single-blind review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers have introduced measures to reduce unfairness, including offering double-blind review or other policies. Awareness of both conscious and unconscious bias is required and policy choices should weigh trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling unethical reviewer behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect and act on reviewers failing to disclose conflicts of interest, misusing confidential information or ideas, engaging in ad hominem criticism, or delaying reviews for competitive advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow COPE guidance and other publisher procedures to investigate and respond to suspected unethical activity. Enhance system checks in reviewer selection and consider removing facilities that allow unchecked author-suggested reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of anonymity model (single-blind vs double-blind vs open)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to use single-blind (authors known to reviewers), double-blind (neither party knows the other's identity) or open review (both identities known), recognising differing trade-offs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-blind is common but open to criticism for bias; double-blind can increase confidence but may be hard to fully anonymise manuscripts; open review may improve accountability but may reduce willingness to review, especially for critical/rejection recommendations. Allowing authors or reviewers opt-in can be a pragmatic approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency through publishing reviews and pre-publication histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish review reports and authors' responses alongside the final article to provide readers with contextual information about the paper's development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can promote honesty and thoroughness. Some journals publish reports without revealing reviewer names; others make naming optional. Uptake and demand vary; publishers and authors can be given choice over revealing pre-publication history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive reviewer-author discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interactive, moderated online discussions (post-initial review) between authors, reviewers and editors to reach a consensus decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Frontiers (two-stage process) and eLife (reviewers discuss reviews with each other and an editor). Such interactions can consolidate comments into a single set of revisions and provide training/feedback for reviewers, but require suitable editorial systems and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing reviews without revealing reviewer names
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the content of reviews public while keeping reviewer identities anonymous when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach provides transparency about the review content while protecting reviewer identities; some journals (e.g., EMBO Journal) follow this model. Authors may be given the option whether their pre-publication history is revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pre-prints and discipline-appropriate caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage rapid dissemination via pre-print servers (e.g., ArXiv) where appropriate, but exercise caution in fields where premature dissemination could cause harm (e.g., clinical/medical contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-prints enable quick feedback and are well-established in some fields; extending the model to others requires consideration of risks from flawed research entering the public domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage publication with public discussion (discussion journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operate a staged process where papers passing basic checks are posted publicly for discussion (anonymous/named comments), then undergo formal peer review for final acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics (ACPD/ACP) and Copernicus journals; both published and accepted versions are citable and archived. This model promotes community input before final peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author and reviewer choices on review transparency (PeerJ model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow reviewers and authors to choose whether reviewer names and reviews are revealed/published, and provide DOIs for public reviews where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PeerJ allows reviewers to reveal names (some do) and authors to opt to publish reviews (most do), assigning DOIs to reviews when made public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid initial checks plus stamped peer-review statuses (F1000Research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish submissions after a basic in-house check with a visible post-publication peer-review status assigned by invited referees (approved / approved with reservations / not approved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F1000Research posts versions with review reports and statuses; indexing (e.g., PubMed) occurs after a specified combination of approval statuses, and all versions/reports are archived in databases like PubMed Central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cascading or portable reviews within and across publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable authors to request that reviews commissioned by one journal be forwarded to another journal to reduce redundant reviewing effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most publishers offer intra-publisher transfer; cross-publisher transfer alliances exist (e.g., Neuroscience Peer Review Consortium) but take-up is small. Transfers should be optional for authors and typically require informing reviewers. Practical and commercial barriers (editor independence, system workflows) remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for editor independence when using transferred reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that receiving editors may be cautious about relying on reviews produced for a different journal and may seek additional reviews to match their journal's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should be cautious about undermining editorial autonomy; transferred reviews can be useful but editors value control over decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: System security and reviewer-selection checks to prevent review fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve editorial management system security and enhance checks on reviewer nominations and identities to guard against bogus or conflicted reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some publishers removed facilities that allowed unchecked author-suggested reviewers; vigilance is needed given high incentives to publish in prestigious journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility as a key goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to improve reproducibility, replicability and reliability of published research; acknowledge many published bioscience studies are not reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use checklists and policies to support reproducibility where appropriate, while recognising reproducibility is not equally achievable across all disciplines and study types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data availability and linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage or require authors to make underlying data available in public repositories and to provide bidirectional links when publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large data volumes make in-depth pre-publication review of data unrealistic for most reviewers; specialist data journals or paid data/informatics reviewers may be needed. Repository deposition improves transparency and post-publication scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist statistical and data review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specialist statistical or data reviewers to assess analyses where appropriate, since many journals lack industry-wide statistical-review guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals recruit or pay specialist reviewers; many do not, contributing to statistical errors in the literature. Publishers may develop reviewer guidance or recruit statistical reviewers selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that post-publication peer review encompasses many practices: invited reviewers after a pre-print, third-party open-review platforms, publisher-hosted post-publication comments, and social-media discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different systems vary in openness, gatekeeping, and uptake. Distinguish between moderated post-publication review by invited experts and open-comment platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of unreviewed public dissemination in sensitive fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious with publish-then-filter models in areas like medicine and life sciences where flawed research can cause harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such models promote rapid dissemination and feedback, publishers and communities should evaluate suitability and add safeguards for clinical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low incentives and uptake for post-publication commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that few researchers engage in post-publication commenting due to lack of incentives, time constraints and risk of alienating colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many publishing platforms report modest take-up; some exceptions (BMJ rapid responses) exist. Consider mechanisms to incentivise and credit post-publication engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying commenter expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure, where possible, that post-publication comments and reviews are made by individuals with relevant expertise, though effective verification is often lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some platforms require ORCID, prior publications, or institutional email; others allow open registration. Lack of robust expertise checks can reduce the reliability of post-publication comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing anonymous commenting and its risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance benefits of anonymity (encouraging candid critique) against risks (defamation, unfair attacks) observed on platforms like PubPeer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity can facilitate criticism but may enable harmful behaviour. Platforms must have policies and moderation processes to address unfair critiques and legal challenges; some resist de-anonymising to protect critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fragmentation and discoverability of post-publication commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that comments and reviews are spread across many platforms (blogs, social media, third-party sites), making it hard to track all discussion related to an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and platforms should consider integration and linking strategies (DOIs, links) to improve discoverability; consolidation may occur around successful services but is not guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and development of post-publication metrics (altmetrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate evidence of article-related activity (comments, social mentions, bookmarks, media coverage) to produce article-level metrics complementing citations and usage data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Services include Altmetric, Plum Analytics, ImpactStory. These metrics are evolving in complexity and may integrate with citation services; publishers are exploring integration with article pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers treating post-publication review as a supplement
rubrics_metrics.description: View post-publication comments, ratings and metrics as an important supplement, but not a replacement, for pre-publication peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers often link to third-party comments and engage with altmetrics providers; further investment and integration will be required for deeper dialogue between pre- and post-publication actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and guidance for editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide information packs, guidance notes, workshops, videos and online courses to support new and existing editors' skills in managing peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers (PLOS, BMJ, Elsevier) use mixed approaches; in-house training and experienced-editor mentorship are common. Investment in editor training improves review quality and system functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and feedback for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer structured or informal training, feedback from editors, workshops, webinars and mentoring programmes for reviewers, especially early-career researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer training is less structured than editor training; some publishers provide feedback and certification for completion of reviewer training. Interactional review models (e.g., eLife) provide valuable reviewer feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewing as mentorship with transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage senior reviewers to involve junior colleagues in reviewing as a training exercise, provided this is done transparently and both contributors are identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency (both reviewers signing the report) helps training while avoiding unethical delegation. Publishers may advertise opportunities to early-career researchers to build reviewer capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify roles of publishers versus institutions/funders in reviewer training
rubrics_metrics.description: Define responsibilities and relationships between publishers’ training initiatives and broader training provided by funders or research institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers wish to expand training but are unclear about overlap with institutional or funder training for PhD students and early-career researchers; coordination may be beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition, credit and reward mechanisms for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop non-monetary recognition (annual lists, subscription/APC discounts, badges, reviewer profiles) and integrate reviews into scholarly credit systems (DOIs, ORCID, Publons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers pilot digital badges, reviewer-recognition platforms, and DOI assignment for published reviews to make reviewing activity more visible and citable. Aggregators like Publons allow reviewers to control display of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about monetising peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about offering monetary payments to reviewers because of cost implications and potential effects on reviewer-editor-author relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments would raise costs passed to institutions and could change incentive structures. Some models (e.g., Collabra) include payments; publishers are watching developments but remain cautious.
